svg.text: reveal(r, c) — THE GUARD LADDER, in order
return false — moves after WON/LOST are ignored, not errors
throw IllegalArgumentException — a caller bug, not a move
return false — a flag is a lock; you must unflag to click
the clicked cell is excluded from the draw ⇒ move 1 cannot lose
return false — the "false" here means lost, not no-op. Overloaded.
status = WON · return true — flags are irrelevant to winning
that win check rescans the whole grid every move: O(R·C) per reveal.
A counter incremented inside the BFS would make it O(1). Say so.
THE FLOOD FILL, WORKED — one click opens a whole region
6×5 board, 3 mines. Player clicks (0,0), which has adjacentMines == 0.
Mines drawn for the reader — in play they are hidden until the game is lost.

svg.text: green = zero cells, popped AND expanded (12 of them)
amber = numbered frontier: revealed, but NOT expanded

One click revealed 18 of 27 safe cells. That asymmetry —
one action, unbounded effect — is the whole game.
A flagged cell inside the region is skipped at pop and blocks
expansion through it — a bad flag can wall off part of the fill.
GameStatus — three states, no way back
the only state that accepts moves
terminal — every later move is a silent no-op
terminal — mines need not be flagged
Both terminals are absorbing: the status check sits at the TOP
of reveal() and toggleFlag(), so nothing can mutate after. ✓
No RESET / restart transition exists — you construct a new
Minesweeper for a new game. Deliberate: nothing to un-place.
Win requires revealing every safe cell; flag count is cosmetic
and never enters the condition. That matches the real game.

g.text: WHY BFS AND NOT RECURSION?
DFS recursion is the obvious first answer and it works fine on a 16×30 expert board.
It stops working the moment the grid gets big: a 1000×1000 board with one huge zero
region gives a recursion depth near 10⁶ and blows the JVM stack.
The iterative version moves that same frontier onto the heap as an ArrayDeque, where
it is bounded by available memory rather than by −Xss. Same O(R·C), no cliff.
BFS vs DFS order does not matter here — every reachable cell ends up revealed either
way. The choice is about the stack, not the traversal order. Say that; it lands well.
THE DUPLICATE-PUSH QUESTION
A cell can be pushed more than once — two different zero
cells share neighbours. There is no visited set.
That is safe because the isRevealed() check happens at POP,
not at push: the second copy is popped and dropped.
Cost is a bounded constant factor on queue size, not on
correctness. The revealed flag IS the visited set — which is
exactly why you do not need a second one.
FOLLOW-UPS THIS DIAGRAM SETS UP
• "Make the win check O(1)" → keep a revealedSafe counter, bump it inside the BFS
instead of rescanning the grid in countRevealedSafeCells().
• "Add chording" → middle-click a number whose flag count matches; reveal its
unflagged neighbours by seeding the SAME queue with all of them. No new algorithm.
• "Make it multiplayer" → now Board needs a lock, and reveal() must be atomic from
the guard ladder through the BFS, or two players race the first-click latch.
• "Guarantee an opening" → exclude the 3×3 around the first click, not just the cell.
